pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 📝 **Strand 2 — Productivity Software**
Sub-strand 1: Introduction to Word Processing

Letters, reports, examination papers, CVs, newspapers and this very textbook were all produced with word processing software. In this unit you will learn why word processors are so important, and how to type, edit, check and format text professionally in Microsoft Word.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B7.2.1.1** Demonstrate how to use Microsoft Word (Editing and Formatting Text).

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B7.2.1.1.1** Explain the importance of word processing software.
- **B7.2.1.1.2** Demonstrate how to insert, select, delete and move text.
- **B7.2.1.1.3** Demonstrate how to find and replace content and undo edited changes.
- **B7.2.1.1.4** Demonstrate how to spell check, carry out content translation and language setting.
- **B7.2.1.1.4.5** Demonstrate how to use text decoration, change text case, text size and colour.
- **B7.2.1.1.4.6** Demonstrate how to align text, indent paragraphs, bullet, line space and shade.
- **B7.2.1.1.3 (Formatting)** Demonstrate how to set tabs and apply formatting.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 4.1 The Importance of Word Processing Software
- 4.2 Inserting, Selecting, Deleting and Moving Text
- 4.3 Find and Replace, Undo and Redo
- 4.4 Spelling and Grammar, Translation and Language Settings
- 4.5 Text Decoration, Case, Size and Colour
- 4.6 Paragraph Formatting: Alignment, Indents, Bullets, Line Spacing, Borders and Shading
- 4.7 Setting Tabs and Applying Formatting

**Core competencies developed:** Communication and Collaboration (CC8.2), Digital Literacy (DL5.1), Creativity and Innovation (CI5.4).

lessons.title: The Importance of Word Processing Software

pages.title: The Importance of Word Processing Software
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain the meaning of a word processor;
- state the importance of word processors;
- name common word processing packages.
A **word processor** is application software used to **create, edit, format, save, share and print** text documents such as letters, essays, reports, minutes, CVs, invitations and newsletters. A document created in a word processor is saved as a file and can be changed at any time without retyping it.
## Importance of word processors
- **Easy editing:** you can insert, delete, move and correct text without retyping the whole document.
- **Professional formatting:** fonts, colours, headings, bullets, tables and pictures make documents attractive and easy to read.
- **Proofing tools:** spelling and grammar checkers, a thesaurus and translation tools improve accuracy.
- **Saving and reusing work:** documents can be stored, copied, used as templates and updated later.
- **Sharing and collaboration:** files can be emailed, shared online and edited by several people at once (e.g. Google Docs, Word for the web).
- **Printing many copies** of the same document, each identical.
- **Special features:** mail merge (personalised letters), page numbers, tables of contents, word count, track changes and comments.

pages.title: Examples of word processing software
pages.body:
## Examples of word processing software
| **Software** | **Developer / notes** |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Word | Microsoft; part of Microsoft 365/Office. The most widely used word processor; saves as .docx |
| Google Docs | Google; free, works in a web browser, saves automatically to Google Drive, real-time collaboration |
| LibreOffice Writer | The Document Foundation; free and open-source; saves as .odt and can open .docx |
| Corel WordPerfect | Corel; part of WordPerfect Office; popular with some law firms |
| AbiWord | Free, lightweight word processor |
| Apple Pages | Apple; free on Mac, iPhone and iPad |
| WordPad and Notepad | Simple programs included with Windows. Notepad edits plain text only (.txt). WordPad was removed from new Windows 11 installations in 2024. |
> 🧪 **Activity — Brainstorm**
In groups, list all the documents your school office produces in one term (e.g. report cards, timetables, letters to parents). Discuss how a word processor helps to produce each one.

lessons.title: Inserting, Selecting, Deleting and Moving Text

pages.title: Inserting, Selecting, Deleting and Moving Text
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- identify the parts of the Microsoft Word interface;
- insert, select, delete and move text;
- use the Insert and Overtype modes.
[[fig:c7-f12|Figure 11: The Microsoft Word window]]
| **Part** | **Purpose** |
|---|---|
| Title bar | Shows the document name and the program name |
| Quick Access Toolbar | Shortcut buttons such as Save, Undo and Redo |
| Ribbon | Tabs (File, Home, Insert, Layout, Review, View, etc.) containing groups of commands |
| Ruler | Shows margins, indents and tab stops |
| Document area | Where you type; the blinking insertion point shows where text will appear |
| Status bar | Shows page number, word count, language and proofing status |
| View buttons and Zoom slider | Change how the document is displayed and its magnification |
## Inserting text
Click where you want the text to appear, then type. Press **Enter** only at the end of a paragraph; Word wraps lines automatically (**word wrap**). Press **Spacebar** once between words.
## Selecting text
| **To select…** | **Do this** |
|---|---|
| A word | Double-click the word |
| A sentence | Hold **Ctrl** and click anywhere in the sentence |
| A paragraph | Triple-click in the paragraph |
| A line | Click in the left margin beside the line |
| Any block of text | Drag across it, or click at the start and **Shift + click** at the end |
| Character by character | **Shift + arrow keys** |
| The whole document | **Ctrl + A** |

pages.title: Deleting text
pages.body:
## Deleting text
- **Backspace** deletes the character to the **left** of the insertion point.
- **Delete** removes the character to the **right** of the insertion point.
- To delete a block, select it and press **Delete** or **Backspace**.
- **Ctrl + Backspace** deletes the whole word to the left.
## Moving and copying text
| **Action** | **Ribbon (Home › Clipboard)** | **Keyboard** | **Mouse** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Move | Cut, then Paste | **Ctrl + X**, then **Ctrl + V** | Drag the selected text to the new position |
| Copy | Copy, then Paste | **Ctrl + C**, then **Ctrl + V** | Hold **Ctrl** while dragging |
## Insert mode and Overtype mode
In **Insert mode** (the normal mode), new text pushes existing text to the right. In **Overtype mode**, new text **replaces** the characters to the right of the insertion point.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Switching on Overtype using the status bar**
1. **Right-click** the status bar at the bottom of the Word window.
2. Click **Overtype** in the list so that it is ticked. The word **Insert** now appears on the status bar.
3. Click the word **Insert** on the status bar to switch to **Overtype**; click it again to return to Insert mode.
4. Optional: to use the **Insert** key on the keyboard as a switch, go to **File › Options › Advanced** and tick **Use the Insert key to control overtype mode**.

pages.title: Deleting text (continued)
pages.body:
> 💻 **Practical session — Edit a paragraph**
1. Type: Ghana is a country in West Africa. Its capital is Accra. Ghana became independent on 6th March, 1957.
2. Select the second sentence and move it to the end of the paragraph.
3. Copy the first sentence and paste it at the end.
4. Delete the copied sentence using Backspace.
5. Switch on Overtype and replace “West” with “east”; observe what happens, then undo it and switch back to Insert.

pages.title: Find and Replace, Undo and Redo
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- use the Find and Replace tools;
- use the Editing group on the Home tab;
- undo and redo changes.
The **Editing group** at the right end of the **Home** tab contains **Find**, **Replace** and **Select**.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Finding text**
1. Click **Home › Editing › Find** (or press **Ctrl + F**). The **Navigation pane** opens on the left.
2. Type the word to look for, e.g. Ghana. Every match is highlighted and listed in the pane, with the number of results.
3. Click a result in the pane to jump to it.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Replacing text**
1. Click **Home › Editing › Replace** (or press **Ctrl + H**).
2. In **Find what**, type the word to change, e.g. colour. In **Replace with**, type the new word, e.g. color.
3. Click **Find Next** to see each match, then **Replace** to change only that one, or **Replace All** to change every match.
4. Click **More >>** for options such as **Match case** and **Find whole words only**.
> ✏️ **Worked example — Why “Find whole words only” matters**
Replacing cat with dog without this option would also change “**cat**egory” into “**dog**egory”.
## Undo and Redo
- **Undo** (**Ctrl + Z**, or the curved-left arrow on the Quick Access Toolbar) reverses your last action. Press it several times to go back several steps.
- **Redo** (**Ctrl + Y**) puts back an action you have undone.
- The **Select** button in the Editing group can select all text, objects or text with similar formatting.

lessons.title: Spelling and Grammar, Translation and Language Settings

pages.title: Spelling and Grammar, Translation and Language Settings
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- check spelling and grammar;
- use the thesaurus;
- translate text and set the proofing language.
The **Review** tab contains the **Proofing** and **Language** groups.
## Spelling and grammar
Word underlines possible spelling errors with a **red wavy line** and grammar or style issues with a **blue double underline**. Right-click an underlined word to see suggestions.
> 🪜 **Step by step — Checking a whole document**
1. Click at the start of the document.
2. Click **Review › Proofing › Spelling & Grammar** (in Microsoft 365 the button is called **Editor**), or press **F7**.
3. For each issue, choose a suggestion, **Ignore Once**, **Ignore All**, or **Add to Dictionary** (for correct names such as “Kwame” or “Tamale”).
> 🛡️ **Safety first — Proofing tools are helpers, not teachers** A spell checker will not catch a correctly spelled wrong word: “Their going to school” has no spelling errors, but it is wrong (They’re). Always proofread your work yourself.
## Thesaurus and word count
Select a word and click **Review › Thesaurus** (**Shift + F7**) to see **synonyms** (words with similar meanings) and antonyms. Click **Word Count** to see the number of pages, words, characters and paragraphs.
## Translation
> 🪜 **Step by step — Translating text**
1. Select the text to translate, e.g. a sentence in English.
2. Click **Review › Language › Translate › Translate Selection** (or **Translate Document** to translate the whole file into a new document).
3. In the **Translator** pane, choose the target language, e.g. **French**. The translation appears; click **Insert** to put it in the document.

pages.title: Spelling and Grammar, Translation and Language Settings (continued)
pages.body:
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY** The Translator in Word supports more than 100 languages, including African languages such as **Hausa**, **Yoruba** and **Swahili**. **Google Translate** also supports Ghanaian languages such as **Twi (Akan)** and **Ewe**. The list of languages keeps growing, so check the drop-down list in the Translator pane. Machine translation is useful but not perfect, so ask a speaker of the language to check important translations.
## Setting the proofing language
> 🪜 **Step by step — Changing the language of the proofing tools**
1. Select the text (or press **Ctrl + A** for the whole document).
2. Click **Review › Language › Language › Set Proofing Language**.
3. Choose **English (United Kingdom)** (Ghana uses British spelling, e.g. colour, centre, organise) and click **OK**. Tick **Set As Default** to use it for new documents.
> ⏳ **Then and now — WHAT YOU WILL SEE TODAY** The curriculum also mentions finding these tools on the **Home** tab. In Microsoft 365, the **Editor** button appears on the right of the **Home** tab, and **Dictate** (speech-to-text) is also on the Home tab. The full set of proofing tools remains on the **Review** tab.

pages.title: Text Decoration, Case, Size and Colour
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- use the Font group on the Home tab;
- change text case, font size and colour;
- apply text decorations.
**Formatting** changes how text looks without changing what it says. Most text formatting is in the **Home › Font** group. Always **select the text first**, then apply the format.
| **Button / command** | **What it does** | **Shortcut** |
|---|---|---|
| Font (typeface) | Changes the style of letters, e.g. Calibri, Times New Roman, Arial | Ctrl + Shift + F |
| Font size | Changes the size of text, measured in points (pt); 72 pt ≈ 2.54 cm | Ctrl + ] / Ctrl + [ |
| Grow / Shrink Font | Increases or decreases the size step by step | Ctrl + Shift + > / < |
| Change Case (Aa) | Sentence case., lowercase, UPPERCASE, Capitalize Each Word, tOGGLE cASE | Shift + F3 |
| Bold / Italic / Underline | **Bold**, italic, underlined text; click the arrow beside U for underline styles | Ctrl + B / I / U |
| Strikethrough | Draws a line through text (used to show deleted items) | — |
| Subscript / Superscript | H₂O (subscript), x² (superscript) | Ctrl + = / Ctrl + Shift + = |
| Text Effects and Typography | Outline, shadow, reflection and glow effects | — |
| Text Highlight Colour | Marks text like a highlighter pen | — |
| Font Colour | Changes the colour of the letters | — |
| Clear All Formatting | Removes all formatting from the selection | Ctrl + Space |
| Font dialog launcher (↘) | Opens the Font dialog box with more options (e.g. small caps, character spacing) | Ctrl + D |

pages.title: Text Decoration, Case, Size and Colour (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know?** **Serif** fonts (like Times New Roman) have small “feet” on the letters and are traditional for printed books. **Sans-serif** fonts (like Calibri and Arial) have no feet and are easier to read on screens.
> 💻 **Practical session — Design a notice**
Type a notice announcing your school’s **Computing Club** meeting. Make the heading UPPERCASE, 24 pt, bold and dark blue. Change the body text to 12 pt Calibri. Underline the date, italicise the venue, and highlight the time in yellow. Write the formula for water as H₂O and the area as 25 m² somewhere in your notice to practise subscript and superscript.

lessons.title: Paragraph Formatting: Alignment, Indents, Bullets, Line Spacing, Borders and Shading

pages.title: Paragraph Formatting: Alignment, Indents, Bullets, Line Spacing, Borders and Shading
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.4
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- align text;
- indent paragraphs and use bullets;
- set line spacing; apply borders and shading.
Paragraph formatting applies to whole paragraphs. You only need to click inside a paragraph (or select several paragraphs) and use the **Home › Paragraph** group.
## Alignment
| **Alignment** | **Effect** | **Shortcut** | **Typical use** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Align Left | Text lines up on the left margin; ragged right edge | Ctrl + L | Most letters and essays |
| Centre | Text is centred between the margins | Ctrl + E | Titles, headings, invitations |
| Align Right | Text lines up on the right margin | Ctrl + R | Dates and addresses in letters |
| Justify | Text lines up on both margins (extra space is added between words) | Ctrl + J | Books, newspapers, reports |
## Indentation
An **indent** is the distance between the text and the margin. Use **Increase Indent** and **Decrease Indent** buttons to move a whole paragraph. In the **Paragraph dialog box** (click the small arrow ↘ at the bottom-right of the Paragraph group) you can set special indents:
- **First line indent:** only the first line moves in (common in novels and essays).
- **Hanging indent:** all lines except the first move in (used in reference lists).
- You can also drag the indent markers on the **ruler**.

pages.title: Bullets and numbering
pages.body:
## Bullets and numbering
**Bullets** list items where order does not matter; **numbering** is for steps or ranked items. Click the arrow beside the Bullets button to choose a different symbol. Press **Tab** to move an item down a level and **Shift + Tab** to move it up.
## Line spacing
Click **Line and Paragraph Spacing** to choose 1.0 (single), 1.15, 1.5, 2.0 (double) and so on, or open the Paragraph dialog box and set **Line spacing** and **Spacing Before/After** precisely.
## Borders and shading
> 🪜 **Step by step — Adding a border and shading to a paragraph**
1. Click inside the paragraph.
2. Click the arrow beside the **Borders** button (Home › Paragraph) and choose **Outside Borders**.
3. For more choices, click **Borders and Shading…** Choose a style, colour and width on the **Borders** tab, then a fill colour on the **Shading** tab. Make sure **Apply to** says **Paragraph**, then click **OK**.
4. For quick shading, click the **Shading** (paint bucket) button and pick a light colour.
> 💻 **Practical session — Format a school announcement**
Type three paragraphs about your school’s Speech and Prize-Giving Day. Centre the title; justify the body; give the first paragraph a 1.27 cm first-line indent; list four activities with bullets; set line spacing to 1.5; and place a blue border with light-grey shading around the final paragraph.

pages.title: Setting Tabs and Applying Formatting
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B7.2.1.1.3
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- explain what tab stops are;
- set left, centre and right tabs;
- use tab stops to line up text in columns.
Pressing the **Tab** key moves the insertion point to the next **tab stop**. By default, Word places tab stops every 1.27 cm (0.5 inch). You can set your own tab stops to line up text neatly in columns, which is much better than pressing the spacebar many times.
[[fig:c7-f13|Figure 12: Left, centre and right tab stops on the ruler]]
| **Tab type** | **Ruler symbol** | **How text lines up** |
|---|---|---|
| Left tab | L | Text starts at the tab stop and extends to the right |
| Centre tab | ⊥ | Text is centred on the tab stop |
| Right tab | ⅃ | Text ends at the tab stop (good for numbers and page numbers) |
| Decimal tab | ⊥ with a dot | Numbers line up on the decimal point |
| Bar tab | / | Draws a vertical line at the tab stop |
> 🪜 **Step by step — Setting tabs with the ruler**
1. Make sure the ruler is visible: **View › Show › Ruler**.
2. Click the **tab selector** at the far left of the horizontal ruler until it shows the tab type you want (e.g. **Centre tab**).
3. Click on the ruler where you want the tab stop (e.g. at 8 cm). Repeat for a **Right tab** at 15 cm.
4. Type the first item, press **Tab**, type the second item, press **Tab**, type the third item, then press **Enter**.
5. To move a tab stop, drag it along the ruler; to remove it, drag it down off the ruler.

pages.title: Setting Tabs and Applying Formatting (continued)
pages.body:
> 🪜 **Step by step — Setting exact tabs with dot leaders (Tabs dialog box)**
1. Open the **Paragraph** dialog box and click **Tabs…**
2. Type a position, e.g. 15 cm, choose **Right** alignment and leader **2 ……**, then click **Set** and **OK**.
3. Type Introduction, press **Tab** and type 1. Dots fill the gap, as in a table of contents.
> 💻 **Practical session — Class list with tabs**
Using a left tab at 0 cm, a centre tab at 8 cm and a right tab at 15 cm, type a list of five classmates with their **Name**, **Class** and **Score**, as shown in the figure. Make the heading row bold.

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Give **five** reasons why word processors are important.
2. Explain the difference between the **Delete** and **Backspace** keys.
3. Describe how to move a sentence using the keyboard.
4. Outline the steps for replacing every occurrence of a word in a document.
5. List **five** options available under Change Case.
6. Explain why tabs are better than spaces for lining up columns of text.
## Practical tasks
1. Type a one-page letter to your District Director of Education inviting him/her to your school’s Computing Club launch. Apply correct alignment, a first-line indent, 1.15 line spacing, bold and underline where appropriate, and check the spelling with English (UK).
2. Translate a three-line welcome message into French using the Translate tool and insert it below the English version.
